findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: The £0.793m pay award pressure (additional 0.3%) is included in the quarter two forecast and carries an ongoing impact on base budgets.
findings.detail: The paper says pay budgets are under considerable stress, compounded by the vacancy factor target. The ongoing cost must be built into base budgets as part of the 2027/28 MTFS.
findings.matters: A pay award above budget adds to every council's base budget going forward, so the size of the gap an additional 0.3% creates is directly comparable across councils.
findings.figures: £0.793m pay award pressure; additional 0.3% pay award
findings.quote: As reported last quarter, the £0.793m pressure associated with the pay award (additional 0.3%) is included within the forecast.

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: Car parking forecasts a £0.961m underspend, a favourable movement of £0.732m from quarter one, with approved tariff increases included.
findings.detail: The paper says car parking usage has stayed in high demand since the tariff increases, continuing a trend from 2025/26 driven by new machines, new payment options and additional enforcement officers. Parking bay suspensions for utility works are also generating income.
findings.matters: It is a clear case of a fees and charges income line beating budget, which other councils budgeting for similar tariff changes can compare against.
findings.figures: £0.961m underspend; £0.732m favourable movement from quarter one
findings.quote: Car Parking services are currently forecasting an underspend of £0.961m

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: £1.500m drawdown from the Treasury Reserve to offset the shortfall in Crisis Resilience Fund funding after the final settlement came in lower than budgeted
findings.detail: Cabinet is asked to approve this drawdown. The Crisis Resilience Fund replaced the Household Support Fund from April 2026, and the paper seeks to move its budget from Finance, Revenues and Benefits to Leisure, Culture & Communities.
findings.matters: A government grant settlement coming in below budget and being covered from a treasury reserve is a funding shortfall other councils running similar grant-funded schemes may face.
findings.figures: £1.500m drawdown from the Treasury Reserve
findings.quote: A drawdown of £1.500m from the Treasury Reserve to offset the shortfall in Crisis Resilience Fund funding

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: The Transformation Reserve is forecast to fall to approximately £0.6m after the council funds over £2.4m of transformation activity from it in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The S151 officer notes that MTFS commitments extend beyond the remaining reserve balance and will need detailed review as future budget proposals are developed. The reserve was partly used to fund the 2024/25 year-end overspend and must be repaid as opportunities arise.
findings.matters: A reserve funding transformation that falls to a small balance while commitments continue constrains how far the council can rely on transformation to close future gaps.
findings.figures: over £2.4m drawn for transformation activity; approximately £0.6m remaining balance
findings.quote: The impact of the drawdown in 2026/27 will result in a balance on the reserve of approximately £0.6m.

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: A £2.220m saving has been identified following restructuring of loans, against a £0.720m net interest overspend.
findings.detail: The net interest overspend reflects a higher interest rate environment than assumed at budget setting. A £1.000m drawdown from the Treasury volatility reserve is proposed to support it. Finance & Investment Income & Expense is forecast at £8.418m against an £11.888m budget.
findings.matters: A loan restructuring that yields a saving at this scale is a specific borrowing action a finance director at another council may want to understand, and it shows how the council is managing interest costs.
findings.figures: £2.220m restructuring saving; £0.720m net interest overspend; £1.000m reserve drawdown; £11.888m budget; £8.418m forecast
findings.quote: A £2.220m saving has been identified following restructuring of loans

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: The council has taken out no new long-term borrowing in 2026/27 so far, but has taken out new short-term loans to cover cashflow.
findings.detail: Some long-term borrowing may be taken towards year end to unwind part of the council's under-borrowed position. The paper also says the DSG deficit will require the council to access financial markets to borrow this financial year, adding interest payable costs.
findings.matters: A move from under-borrowing to market borrowing would change the council's funding need, which lenders and peers with similar DSG exposure will track.
findings.figures: no new long-term borrowing in 2026/27 to 30 September 2026; £90.3m Safety Valve grant expected 30 November 2026
findings.quote: the Council has not taken out any new long-term borrowing (loans) during 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: The S151 officer estimates the council will need to find approximately £10m for the DSG deficit by 31 March 2028, assuming government support for 90% of the deficit.
findings.detail: The paper says the council would not have sufficient reserves to fund the predicted cumulative deficit if the High Needs Sustainability plan and government reforms do not deliver and the override is not extended. It also notes the council is not alone nationally on this issue.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can compare this approximately £10m exposure against the council's available reserves, which the paper says are sufficient for the current year only.
findings.figures: approximately £10m; 90% government support assumed; 31 March 2028
findings.quote: will need to find approximately £10m to cover this by 31 March 2028

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: The council expects a High Needs Stability Grant of £90.326m at the end of November 2026, leaving a £3.942m surplus to set against deficits before the statutory override ends.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit at the end of 2025/26 was £86.384m after Safety Valve payments and the agreed council contribution. The surplus arises because the council's Safety Valve contribution was higher than the 10% required under the new grant conditions. The paper says government arrangements for deficits accrued in 2026/27 and 2027/28 are not yet confirmed.
findings.matters: The grant and the £3.942m surplus determine how much of the cumulative deficit the council must fund itself, which is the central question for peers with DSG deficits and for anyone lending against them.
findings.figures: £90.326m estimated grant; £3.942m surplus; £86.384m DSG deficit at end of 2025/26; 31 March 2028 override end date
findings.quote: This £3.942m will be set aside to offset deficits accrued before the end of the statutory override period (31st March 2028).

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: The DSG deficit is forecast to be £1.458m higher than the Local SEND Reform Plan submitted to the DfE, with the high needs block forecast to overspend by £5.785m.
findings.detail: An early years underspend of £5.698m reduces the overall deficit. The high needs overspend rose by £1.410m from quarter one, and the paper says further action is being taken to contain it, including validation of placement and support costs before quarter three.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is the largest single risk the paper identifies, and the gap to the submitted plan is a direct measure of whether the council is on track with the DfE-approved recovery plan.
findings.figures: £5.785m high needs overspend; £5.698m early years underspend; £1.458m above submitted plan; £1.410m adverse movement from quarter one; £68.984m planned in-year deficit
findings.quote: will be £1.458m higher than the submitted plan

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: SEN Transport forecasts a £0.521m overspend, with pupil numbers 6.8% below budget and average cost per pupil 9.4% above.
findings.detail: The forecast of 2,437 pupils is 177 below budget, a favourable £1.799m, but higher average costs add £2.330m, leaving a net overspend. The paper attributes cost increases to route costs, pupil needs, fuel and market capacity. Appendix A gives the overspend as £0.531m, against £0.521m in the main report.
findings.matters: It shows a transport cost base moving with the market rather than with demand, and the planned April 2027 re-tender is the council's next lever on that cost.
findings.figures: £0.521m overspend (main report); £0.531m (Appendix A); 2,437 pupils; 177 (6.8%) below budget assumption; £1.799m favourable volume variance; £11,121 average cost per pupil; £956 (9.4%) above budget; £2.330m adverse cost variance; £0.961m savings target; £0.350m delivered
findings.quote: The forecast average cost per pupil is £11,121, £956 (9.4%) above budget

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: Adult Services forecasts a £1.424m overspend, with £2.057m of pressure in Whole Life Pathway care budgets.
findings.detail: The overspend sits in Whole Life Pathway services for people with learning disabilities, autism and mental health conditions, including LDAS and Moving On services for young people transitioning to adult care. It is partly offset by underspends in Reablement (£0.315m) and Housing Migration & Resettlement (£0.205m), both from vacancies.
findings.matters: Transition-age care demand is a pressure many councils report, and the paper's figures show how it feeds into an overall adult social care forecast.
findings.figures: £1.424m overspend; £2.057m Whole Life Pathway; £0.315m Reablement underspend; £0.205m Housing Migration underspend; £10.038m savings target; £1.302m amber; £1.097m red
findings.quote: The volume of young adults accessing social care services is growing, with pressure on budgets driven by complexity of individual needs.

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: Family & Children Services forecasts a £2.416m overspend, an adverse movement of £2.070m from quarter one.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the movement to a small number of unplanned high-cost placements that were not budgeted for. Placement overspends are forecast at £3.346m, partly offset by a £1m underspend from the cessation of the CSC Prevention Grant, which the paper says has no net impact on the council.
findings.matters: Placement costs in a demand-led service are a common source of in-year overspend, and the forecast shows how a small number of high-cost placements can move a service's position by more than £2m in one quarter.
findings.figures: £2.416m overspend; £2.070m adverse movement; £3.346m placement overspend; £1m CSC Prevention Grant underspend; 492 children we care for against a budgeted 476
findings.quote: The adverse movement of the £2.070m from quarter one is driven by a small number of unplanned high-cost placements that were not budgeted for.

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: The Section 151 officer describes the quarter two financial position as "not tolerable".
findings.detail: The S151 officer states that the Council has sufficient reserves to manage the current year, but that drawing on the General Fund Reserve to fund the overspend is not acceptable given the savings already in the MTFS for future years.
findings.matters: It shows the S151 officer's stated position on whether the overspend can be funded from the General Fund, which a finance director elsewhere or a lender will weigh against the reserve position.
findings.figures: £4.282m forecast overspend
findings.quote: The overall financial position as forecast at Q2 is not tolerable, nor indeed sustainable going forward in the long run.

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: 77% of the £27.807m 2026/27 savings target is reported as achieved or on track at quarter two.
findings.detail: £12.8m (46.20%) is assessed as fully delivered at the end of September and £8.8m (31.79%) is forecast to be achieved by year end. £3.8m (13.76%) is forecast not to be achievable this year and is included as overspends in service forecasts.
findings.matters: Savings delivery is the main driver of this year's position, and any undelivered amount carries into future years' budget gaps, which peers and lenders track.
findings.figures: £27.807m savings target; £12.8m (46.20%) fully delivered; £8.8m (31.79%) forecast achieved by year end; £2.3m (8.25%) with some deliverability risk; £3.8m (13.76%) not forecast achievable this year
findings.quote: The Council is demonstrating delivery in savings with 77% being achieved or on track.

findings.paper_title: Q2 Revenue Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: Wiltshire forecasts a net overspend of £4.282m for 2026/27 at quarter two, a favourable movement of £2.466m from the quarter one forecast of £6.748m.
findings.detail: The forecast is based on information known at 30 September 2026. Children & Education forecasts £2.937m over budget and Care & Wellbeing £1.151m over, with Place forecasting a £1.340m underspend.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how a £4.282m (0.75%) quarter two forecast is being closed, and a lender can see the size of the in-year gap the council must fill from reserves or savings.
findings.figures: £4.282m (0.75% of net budget); £6.748m at quarter one; £2.466m favourable movement; £567.948m net budget; £2.937m Children & Education overspend; £1.151m Care & Wellbeing overspend; £1.340m Place underspend
findings.quote: This quarter two position forecasts a net overspend for the year of £4.282m (0.75% of net budget).

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: The Council operated within its treasury and prudential indicators in the half year to 30 September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says no future difficulties are envisaged in complying with the indicators for the current or future years.
findings.matters: Compliance with the authorised limit and operational boundary is a basic test that finance directors and lenders check each year.
findings.figures: Authorised limit £940.335m; operational boundary £921.445m; borrowing £582.662m
findings.quote: During the half year ended 30 September 2026, the Council has operated within the treasury and prudential indicators

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: The Council's external borrowing is £582.662m, with a net internal borrowing position of £219.245m at 30 September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper describes internal borrowing as cost-effective in the current climate of rising gilt rates. It says the position may need to reduce as interest rates fall.
findings.matters: A council holding over £219m of internal borrowing, with a stated plan to reduce it, is a position other councils and lenders would compare against their own.
findings.figures: £582.662m external borrowing; £219.245m under-borrowed position; £801.907m CFR; £182m under-borrowed in Table 5 is not stated
findings.quote: Table 5 above shows the Council currently has external borrowings of £582.662m and has a net internal borrowing position of £219.245m.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: The paper restates the under-12-months maturity limit at 42.50%, up from 25.00%, while 39.87% of debt currently matures within 12 months.
findings.detail: The paper says advice from MUFG to avoid longer-term loans, given current interest rates, has put pressure on the maturity limits. The limits are to be reviewed every six months.
findings.matters: A council loosening its under-12-months limit to hold more short-term debt is a borrowing policy change other councils and lenders would track.
findings.figures: £232.302m debt maturing under 12 months (39.87%); current limit 25.00%; proposed upper limit 42.50%; total debt £582.662m
findings.quote: The Treasury Management Strategy Statement (TMSS) 2026/27 states that the percentage of debt maturing in under 1 year should not exceed 25%.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: The paper forecasts a borrowing need in February and March 2027, when £53m of PWLB loans mature.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the cash low point mainly to capital programme funding, with lower council tax receipts also expected. It plans to fund the shortfall with PWLB loans, preferably at the lower HRA rate, and temporary loans.
findings.matters: A forecast borrowing need in the months after £53m of PWLB maturities would be a refinancing requirement a lender and peer finance team would see as near-term.
findings.figures: £53m PWLB loans maturing in 2026/27 year end; £45m maturing 23 February 2027; £8m maturing 28 March 2027; £135m temporary loans maturing this financial year, of which £40m in June 2027
findings.quote: We are forecasting a borrowing need to occur in February and March.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: Revised CFR for 2026/27 is £801.907m, against an original estimate of £895.037m, and revised capital expenditure is £212.644m against £260.387m budgeted.
findings.detail: The paper says the lower CFR reflects a reduction in the external borrowing needed for the capital programme. Revised borrowing requirement is £62.294m against £96.503m originally. General Fund capital expenditure is forecast at £163.820m against £212.030m.
findings.matters: A large reduction in planned capital expenditure and borrowing need is a reprofiling a finance director would want to see against their own capital programme.
findings.figures: CFR £801.907m revised vs £895.037m original; capital expenditure £212.644m revised vs £260.387m original; borrowing requirement £62.294m revised vs £96.503m original; General Fund capital £163.820m vs £212.030m
findings.quote: The revised CFR is lower than the original estimate due to the reduction in the external borrowing required to support the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: The investment portfolio yield for the first six months was 3.86%, against a benchmark of 3.73%.
findings.detail: The paper says the Council outperformed the SONIA benchmark by 0.13%. It forecasts £6.1m of interest receivable for 2026/27, with a saving of £0.99m against budget.
findings.matters: A council beating its treasury benchmark while holding £64m of treasury investments is a return figure peers can use to compare their own performance.
findings.figures: 3.86% yield; 3.73% benchmark; 0.13% outperformance; £64m total treasury investments; £6.1m forecast interest receivable; £0.99m saving in budget
findings.quote: The investment portfolio yield for the first six months of the year was 3.86% against a benchmark of 3.73%

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: The CCLA property fund, held at £20m, is valued at £16.483m, with the difference held in an unusable reserve under a statutory override extended to 31 March 2029.
findings.detail: The paper says the fall in value does not currently affect the revenue account. The override applies to existing investments, including this one. The fund produced a net return of 3.82% for the first quarter.
findings.matters: Councils holding property funds have been watching the IFRS 9 override, and an extension to 2029 with a valuation below cost is a point other finance teams would compare.
findings.figures: £20m investment; £16.483m current valuation; net return 3.82%; £0.191m dividend income; override extended to 31 March 2029
findings.quote: Due to a fall in property prices, the fund is currently valued at £16.483m.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: Two debt rescheduling options are being pursued, expected to produce a net benefit of circa £2m in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper says no debt rescheduling has been undertaken to date in 2026/27. It says the two options are still being pursued at the time of writing.
findings.matters: A council pursuing rescheduling for a net benefit, while also repaying PWLB loans early, is a live debt management strategy that peers and lenders would track.
findings.figures: circa £2m net benefit in 2026/27; two options under consideration
findings.quote: However, at the time of writing, the Council is currently pursuing two options that should result in a net benefit to the Council of Circa £2m in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: The paper says the High Needs DSG deficit is having an 'ever-increasing impact' on the cash held by the council.
findings.detail: The paper states that the Council's under-borrowed position will not be maintainable indefinitely. It says a careful balance is being managed to limit the need for borrowing, and that advice will be sought on short- and long-term options.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council with a growing high-needs deficit would find this a direct statement of how the deficit is affecting treasury cash.
findings.figures: Under-borrowed position £219.245m at 30 September 2026
findings.quote: the impact of the increasing deficit in the High Needs Dedicated Schools Grant is having an ever-increasing impact on the cash held by the council.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: Interest of £7.440m accrued on Stone Circle loans remains unpaid, with loans forecast to reach £88.341m by 31 March 2027.
findings.detail: The paper says accrued interest is not being paid in cash, which creates a cash financing cost for the Council. Financing the accrued interest is estimated at £0.394m per year. The paper says delayed Stone Circle interest payments would increase cash flow pressure and credit risk.
findings.matters: Loans to a council-owned company that accrue interest without cash payment are a credit and cash exposure that finance directors and lenders would want to see quantified.
findings.figures: £7.440m accrued interest; £0.394m per annum financing cost; £80.491m loans outstanding at 31 March 2026; £88.341m forecast at 31 March 2027; £7.850m budgeted 2026/27 expenditure
findings.quote: Interest due from Stone Circle has been accrued but remains unpaid, resulting in a cash financing cost to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: Temporary borrowing rose from £100.000m at 31 March 2026 to £175.000m at 30 September 2026, with the average rate on temporary borrowing falling from 4.95% to 4.51%.
findings.detail: The paper says the new short-term borrowing was taken to bridge cashflow deficits, because longer-term rates are higher than expected. It also says the treasury team's planning has lowered the average rate on temporary borrowing.
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing from other councils at this scale, rolled to fund a SEND deficit, is a funding strategy that other councils and lenders would compare.
findings.figures: £100.000m temporary borrowing at 31 March 2026; £175.000m at 30 September 2026; average rate 4.95% falling to 4.51%; £135m of temporary loans maturing this financial year; £4.566m annual loan interest on short-term loans
findings.quote: Due to the overall financial position and the underlying need to borrow for capital purposes (the CFR), new short term external borrowing of £175m was undertaken.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: The paper expects a £90.5m SEND-related grant on 30 November 2026, to repay short-term loans maturing in November and December.
findings.detail: The grant is subject to audit. The paper says it will be used to repay short-term loans from other local authorities maturing in December. Paragraph 41 gives the amount as £90.3m and the main use as £75m of temporary loans maturing in November and December.
findings.matters: A council relying on a single grant to repay £75m of maturing short-term loans, with the amount reported differently in two places, is a funding timing point a lender or peer finance team would track.
findings.figures: £90.5m grant (para 17); £90.3m grant (para 41); £75m of temporary loans to be repaid; payment date 30 November 2026
findings.quote: We have confirmation subject to audit of a £90.5m grant related to the SEND deficit to be paid on 30th November.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: Q2 forecast shows interest payable £1.707m over budget, partly offset by a £0.987m saving on interest receivable.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the interest payable overspend to higher interest rates than expected at budget setting and to extra demand from the SEND deficit. The net interest overspend is £0.72m, which the Council plans to fund with a £1m movement from treasury reserves.
findings.matters: The paper links an interest overspend directly to SEND deficit borrowing demand, which other councils with similar high-needs deficits would recognise.
findings.figures: £1.707m interest payable overspend; £0.987m interest receivable saving; £0.72m net interest overspend; £1m transfer from treasury reserves; £17.438m forecast interest payable; £6.065m forecast interest receivable
findings.quote: Compared to Budget, the Q2 (Midyear) forecast is predicting we will overspend by £1.707m on Interest payable by the Council.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: The Q2 forecast shows an overall £2.47m saving against budget.
findings.detail: The overall figure takes account of the £2.22m early repayment saving, a £1m transfer from treasury reserves, and a £0.03m Monkton Park PFI overspend. The paper notes the interest overspend is offset by these items.
findings.matters: A treasury budget that is forecast to come in under budget after drawing on reserves shows where the offset comes from, which other councils managing similar interest pressures would want to compare.
findings.figures: £2.47m saving against budget; £2.22m early repayment saving; £1m transfer from treasury reserves; £0.03m Monkton Park PFI overspend
findings.quote: the overall forecast position is a £2.47m saving against budget.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: Q2 forecast includes a £2.22m saving in 2026/27 from the proposed early repayment of two £20m PWLB loans.
findings.detail: The saving comes from the discount the PWLB gives on early repayment of fixed-rate loans whose interest rates are well below current PWLB rates. The paper describes the repayment as proposed, not completed.
findings.matters: Early repayment of PWLB debt at a discount is an unusual saving, and other councils holding older fixed-rate PWLB loans may be looking at the same option.
findings.figures: £2.22m saving in 2026/27; two £20m PWLB loans
findings.quote: we have also included £2.22m of savings in 2026/27 arising from the proposed early repayment of two £20m PWLB Loans.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Report on Treasury Management Strategy 261118
findings.headline: The Council's £10m LOBO loan has a lender option date in December 2026, and the paper says the Council would repay its principal if the rate rises above PWLB rates.
findings.detail: The paper says there is a reasonable risk the lender will exercise its option in December. It states the Council will repay the principal if the rate rises above PWLB rates, as this is better value for money. The paper does not say the option has been exercised.
findings.matters: A LOBO call is a repayment and replacement event, so the Council would need to fund £10m from another source, and a finance director at another council would want to see the replacement cost.
findings.figures: £10m LOBO; 4.45% coupon; original maturity 10/12/2052; lender PBB Deutsche Pfandbriefbank; option date December 2026
findings.quote: There is a reasonable risk that the lender will exercise their option in December.

findings.paper_title: Q2 Capital Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: Stone Circle's 280-property portfolio has 265 active tenancies, 94.6% occupancy against a 90% target.
findings.detail: The paper reports that occupancy is above target and that the void rate fell to 5.4% on a stock basis. It also reports the loan balance outstanding to Stone Circle at 31 March 2026 was £80.491m.
findings.matters: Occupancy above target supports rental income that services the council's loan to its housing company, which is a credit point for anyone exposed to that loan.
findings.figures: 265 active tenancies (94.6%); 280 properties; 90% occupancy target; 5.4% void rate; £80.491m loan balance at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: above the occupancy target of 90%.

findings.paper_title: Q2 Capital Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: £0.413m drawn back from future years for the Wiltshire & Swindon History Centre, partly reversing a £0.520m move made at quarter one.
findings.detail: The paper says the heating, cooling, ventilation and humidification work cannot be delayed and must be delivered in 2026/27 to maintain service continuity. It describes the reversal as an example of the challenges of forecasting.
findings.matters: A reversal of a prior reprofiling decision shows how forecast timing can change within one year, which is relevant to anyone judging programme forecasts.
findings.figures: £0.413m drawn back; £0.520m moved to future years at quarter one
findings.quote: This is a partial reversal of the decision to move £0.520m to future years at quarter one

findings.paper_title: Q2 Capital Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: ICT core-network replacement budget of £0.650m moved to future years because procurement is taking longer than planned.
findings.detail: The paper says the core-network replacement is now unlikely to be incurred by 31 March 2027, due to technical definition and procurement timescales. It adds that preparatory work continues, and the reprofiling will cause MRP slippage into later years.
findings.matters: Procurement-driven slippage on borrowing-funded ICT schemes delays both spend and the MRP charge, which affects multi-year revenue planning.
findings.figures: £0.650m moved to future years
findings.quote: Therefore £0.650m has been moved to future years.

findings.paper_title: Q2 Capital Budget Monitoring 261118
findings.headline: The DfT has not included funding for the A350 Melksham Bypass in current plans, and £1.500m has moved to future years.
findings.detail: Following a review of the Major Road Network and Large Local Majors programme, the DfT confirmed the scheme's funding is not in current plans. The paper says further consideration will determine next steps and the impact on the budget line.
findings.matters: A major scheme losing its funding assumption, with its cost still unresolved, is the kind of capital risk peers and lenders will want to see reported.
findings.figures: £1.500m moved to future years

findings.headline: Children's accommodation in-year overspend driven by insufficient local supply and market price escalation
findings.detail: The council is overspending on children's accommodation placements due to insufficient local supply of Independent Fostering Agencies, children's homes, and support provision. Market pressures—including regulatory costs, insurance, and workforce inflation—are driving up individual care package costs, particularly when frameworks are recommissioned. Out-of-county spot purchases are made at higher cost. Two of four planned children's homes have opened and 11 of 14 supported accommodation properties are in procurement, but the current budget remains under pressure.
findings.matters: In-year overspend on a statutory social care function suggests either demand is materially above budget or the council cannot meet need within budget due to market constraints outside its control.
findings.figures: Two of four children's homes opened; 11 of 14 supported accommodation properties in procurement
findings.quote: The budget remains a challenge, with overspend for Children's Accommodation in-year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Strategic Risk Summary - Q1 2026-27
findings.headline: Council's high needs reserve insufficient to meet DSG deficit projected by statutory override end-date of March 2028
findings.detail: Overspend on SEND provision is exceeding the High Needs Block allocation. A SEND Reform Plan submitted to the Department for Education will write off 90% of the DSG deficit as at 31 March 2026, with the remaining 10% to be met from the high needs earmarked reserve. However, the council states its reserve will not cover the cumulative deficit projected by March 2028, when the government's statutory override ends. No government guidance has yet explained how residual deficits accumulated between March 2026 and March 2028 will be managed.
findings.matters: A material statutory function facing cumulative deficits beyond available reserves signals either that the government's funding arrangement is insufficient or that the council's reserve position is structurally weak.
findings.figures: 90% deficit write-off from SEND Reform Plan; 10% from reserves; statutory override deadline March 2028
findings.quote: The council's earmarked reserve is not sufficient to meet the projected deficit at the end of the statutory override.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council and Pension Fund Audit progress report and sector update
findings.headline: Pension Fund audit progressing on schedule with Audit Findings Report delivered to committee

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council and Pension Fund Audit progress report and sector update

This reflects the council's extended audit recovery from prior-year difficulties and the need to rebuild assurance gradually across multiple financial statement areas.
findings.matters: Extended audit timelines and large sample sizes increase audit costs and internal resource burden; they also reflect ongoing confidence deficits from prior-year audit findings.

findings.detail: Auditors are required under the Code of Audit Practice to assess whether the council has made proper arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness. The work is in progress but has faced delays in receiving necessary information. Auditors remain hopeful of reporting findings in the Auditor's Annual Report in November 2026, but the delay indicates information management or resource issues.
findings.matters: Value for Money assessment is a key audit output assessing financial sustainability, governance, and efficiency; delays in completing it may affect the audit opinion timeline and indicate internal coordination or data access issues.

findings.headline: Expenditure cycle identified as significant audit risk due to prior control weaknesses
findings.detail: The auditors did not rebut the expenditure recognition risk for the council due to control issues identified in prior years. Completeness of expenditure has therefore been marked as a significant risk. Sample testing is underway to address both the accuracy and occurrence of expenditure as well as the completeness risk.
findings.matters: Expenditure recognition is a fundamental financial statement area; prior-year control issues that required risk escalation indicate either process gaps or control design deficiencies that affect the reliability of expenditure recording.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council and Pension Fund Audit progress report and sector update
findings.headline: PFI models remain non-compliant with IFRS 16 accounting standard and are under review
findings.detail: IFRS 16 leases became mandatory for local government bodies from 1 April 2024. Auditors' experts are currently reviewing 2025/26 models to track progress against actions from 2024/25. The standard remains unresolved into the second year of its mandatory application.
findings.matters: IFRS 16 is a mandatory accounting standard; failure to implement it affects the accuracy of lease liability recognition and asset valuation in the balance sheet.

findings.detail: The council replaced its cash management system from Civica to Paysuite in March 2026. While auditors found no issues with data completeness or system functionality, IT audit colleagues identified control weaknesses around segregation of duties and made recommendations for improvement to management.

findings.headline: Cash balances misstatement of £21 million from 2024/25 audit remains unadjusted
findings.detail: The auditors identified a £21 million unadjusted misstatement in cash balances in their 2024/25 report and expected the balance to require restatement with a full prior period adjustment. This adjustment has not been made. The issue persists into 2025/26 audit work, which faces delays in completion due to third-party confirmation requests not being received because council signatories have not been updated.
findings.matters: An unadjusted prior-year misstatement of this scale affects the reliability of reported cash positions and indicates unresolved audit findings that carry forward to the current audit.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Pension Fund Audit Findings Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Investment reclassification of £53.069 million from Level 3 to Level 2 in fair value hierarchy classification
findings.detail: Following audit challenge of fair value hierarchy classifications, one investment (NINETY ONE EMTD GBP) valued at £53.069m was reclassified from Level 3 (valuations based on unobservable inputs) to Level 2 (valuations based on observable inputs). The fund manager confirmed this year that Level 2 classification was appropriate. This change affects Note 14a presentation but does not impact the valuation of the investment itself. Prior year comparatives were not restated as the asset was immaterial in prior year. The auditor noted this reclassification issue has been recurring over prior years and the fund continues to keep this under review.
findings.matters: Fair value hierarchy levels indicate the reliability of valuations to users of financial statements. Level 2 is more observable and generally more reliable than Level 3. A significant single reclassification suggests prior control issues but also shows the fund is responding to audit findings. For employers and lenders, accurate classification is important for assessing valuation certainty.
findings.figures: NINETY ONE EMTD GBP investment £53.069m reclassified; prior issue identified in 2023/24 and 2024/25 audits
findings.quote: an investment classified in the draft accounts as Level 3, would be more appropriately classified as Level 2. The value of this investment was £53,069k and it impacts the Private debt row in the Note 14a table

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Pension Fund Audit Findings Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Investment transaction reporting included £172 million of non-trading items recorded as purchases or sales, later corrected
findings.detail: Audit testing of investments identified that Note 12a included transaction activity that were not genuine purchases or sales. A Greencoat investment migration (£100.171m) was incorrectly recorded as both a purchase and sale. Two interfund transfers totalling £72.003m were also incorrectly recorded as purchases and sales. Additionally, an interfund transfer worth £63.203m was misclassified between Infrastructure and Private Debt funds. Although these items were equal and opposite in value (no net impact on investment totals), they overstated gross purchases and sales figures and distorted asset classification. Management agreed to implement regular review processes to identify and exclude non-trading transactions.
findings.matters: Overstated gross transaction volumes obscure true portfolio activity and turnover, even if net valuations are correct. These errors suggest transaction review processes require strengthening. For employers and trustees reviewing fund performance, accurate reporting of portfolio activity is important for understanding manager performance and fees.
findings.figures: Greencoat migration £100.171m; interfund transfers £72.003m; reclassification between asset classes £63.203m and £66.390m
findings.quote: due to the migration of a Greencoat investment for a total of £100,171k from a Colmore system to an AssetMatrix system, a purchase and sale was recorded for this asset, however no purchase or sale occurred and therefore both totals were overstated by this amount. The second finding was due to two interfund transfers being processed as purchases and sales, for a total value of £72,003k.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Pension Fund Audit Findings Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Oracle Fusion control deficiency: four users able to self-assign system access roles without documented approval
findings.detail: The IT audit identified that four users were able to assign roles and profiles to themselves during the audit period without documented approval, request forms, or approval emails. This increases the risk of unauthorised access and inappropriate segregation of duties. The four users did not have access to post to the Pension Fund ledger (access was limited to Council functions), mitigating immediate risk. Management has agreed to implement formal access control procedures requiring documented approval and periodic review of user access.
findings.matters: Self-assigned access without approval is a fundamental control weakness that could permit fraudulent or erroneous activity. While this instance did not affect the Pension Fund directly, the absence of segregation-of-duties controls undermines the control environment and is the type of finding that lenders and employers would expect to see remediated.
findings.figures: 4 users identified with self-assignment capability
findings.quote: Four users were able to assign roles and profiles to themselves during the audit period without documented approval, as no supporting evidence such as request forms or approval emails was available. This increases the risk of unauthorised access, inappropriate segregation of duties, and potential undetected fraudulent or erroneous activity.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Pension Fund Audit Findings Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Unmodified audit opinion anticipated for Wiltshire Pension Fund financial statements for year ended 31 March 2026
findings.detail: Grant Thornton anticipates issuing an unmodified audit opinion on the Pension Fund's financial statements. The audit was substantially completed June-September 2026. No unadjusted misstatements exceeding the reporting threshold of £3.39m were identified. Several disclosure adjustments were made but these do not affect the reported financial position. Work remains outstanding on Level 2 and Level 3 investment valuations, IAS 19 assurance letters, and management representation letters.
findings.matters: An unmodified opinion signals the financial statements give a true and fair view and have been properly prepared. For lenders and employers in the fund, this confirms the fund's reported position is reliable.
findings.figures: Reporting threshold £3.39m; Materiality £67.80m (1.8% of gross investment assets)
findings.quote: Our anticipated financial statements audit report opinion will be unmodified.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Wiltshire SEND Reform Plan - May 2026 (1)
findings.headline: Special school populations have increased 63% since 2019 while mainstream has grown only 2%, with heavy reliance on expensive independent placements
findings.detail: The council notes that mainstream pupil growth is only 2% since 2019 compared to 63% growth in special schools. Wiltshire has comparatively low special school capacity and continued reliance on out-of-area independent placements. This is explicitly identified as creating financial and sufficiency pressure.
findings.matters: Out-of-area independent placements cost significantly more than local provision; heavy reliance indicates substantial, ongoing budget pressure that affects reserve stability

findings.detail: The council identifies sustained demand pressure driven by continued growth in EHCPs, particularly in neurodevelopmental and Social Emotional Mental Health (SEMH) needs. The five-year increase is concentrated in SEMH, speech/language/communication needs, and autism, which together account for 88.8% of all growth.

The S151 flags that 'the cost of delivering HR to schools is currently not cost effective' and an audit is underway to assess this service line.

findings.quote: Risks remain in the service in relation to the traded income targets and the cost of delivering HR to schools is currently not cost effective, this is currently being audited and will need further consideration.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 202526 - Quarter One Revenue Budget Monitoring - Master Report (1)
findings.headline: SEN transport costs rising per pupil by 7.4% (£756 per child) despite lower volumes, due to fuel and market capacity constraints
findings.detail: SEN Transport forecast overspend of £0.369m. Pupil numbers are 147 lower than budget (-5.6%), generating £1.494m favourable variance, but average cost per pupil rises to £10,921 vs budget £10,165 (£756 increase, 7.4%), creating £1.865m adverse variance. Drivers include route cost increases, fuel inflation, market capacity constraints, and increased pupil needs complexity.
findings.matters: Rising per-unit costs despite lower demand indicates capacity constraints and inflationary pressures outside council control; savings targets in this area appear unachievable.

findings.quote: The increase in unit costs more than offsets the savings from lower pupil numbers, leading to a net forecast overspend of £0.369m. The underlying cost pressures are driven by increased route costs, changes in pupil needs and provision requirements, fuel cost inflationary pressures within transport contracts, and market capacity challenges

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 202526 - Quarter One Revenue Budget Monitoring - Master Report (1)
findings.headline: Interest rate environment driving £1.09m net overspend; volatility reserve being drawn to mask unhedged exposure
findings.detail: The council faces £1.09m (net) overspend on interest receivable/payable, described as 'reflective of the higher interest rate environment compared to the estimates used at budget setting'. A £1.000m drawdown from the Treasury Management Volatility Reserve is proposed to offset. A formal review of borrowing and investment portfolio is deferred to Q2/Q3.
findings.matters: Unhedged exposure to interest rates is eroding reserves rather than being managed through debt strategy, suggesting either inadequate treasury hedging or lack of forward visibility in borrowing plans.
findings.figures: £1.09m net interest overspend; £1.000m volatility reserve drawdown proposed
findings.quote: The overspend for interest receivable/payable of £1.09m (net) is reflective of the higher interest rate environment compared to the estimates used at budget setting. A reserve drawdown of £1.000m from the volatility reserve is proposed to support this pressure.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 202526 - Quarter One Revenue Budget Monitoring - Master Report (1)
findings.headline: Transformation Reserve depleting from £2.905m to £0.437m with forward MTFS commitments already exceeding remaining balance
findings.detail: The council is drawing £2.129m from Transformation Reserve in 2026/27, leaving only £0.437m. The S151 Officer flags that 'There are commitments in the MTFS that extend beyond the Reserve balance which will require detailed review as the budget proposals for future years are developed'—indicating committed spend cannot be funded.
findings.matters: Depletion of transformation capacity reserves limits the council's ability to invest in efficiency or manage future one-off costs, while forward commitments exceed available resources.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 202526 - Quarter One Revenue Budget Monitoring - Master Report (1)
findings.headline: Pay award adds unbudgeted £0.793m (0.3%) in 2026/27 and rolls into future year base budgets, worsening budget gaps

This creates structural deficit in future years: the S151 Officer confirms it 'has an on-going impact on the future years base budgets' and notes it increases the already-identified budget gaps of £1.109m (2027/28) and £5.701m (2028/29).
findings.matters: Unbudgeted pay costs that persist into forward years compound the MTFS budget gap and reduce flexibility for future service decisions.
findings.figures: £0.793m in-year; forward gaps £1.109m (2027/28) and £5.701m (2028/29) before this impact

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 202526 - Quarter One Revenue Budget Monitoring - Master Report (1)
findings.headline: DSG deficit escalating; council facing ~£50m in-year overspend and will require external borrowing to manage cash
findings.detail: The High Needs Block forecasts £4.375m overspend on top of a £86.384m opening deficit. The S151 Officer warns 'The deficit is escalating more significantly than originally anticipated, with an additional overspend resulting in a total in-year overspend in the region of £50m.' This cash drain means 'the Council will need access financial markets to borrow this financial year which will result in additional interest payable costs.'
findings.matters: The need to access debt markets due to DSG deficit pressures—rather than genuine capital investment—signals refinancing risk and weakening credit position. If government override is not extended or reforms fail, 'Council will not have sufficient reserves to fund the predicted cumulative deficit.'
findings.figures: £4.375m current year HNB overspend; ~£50m total escalation; opening deficit £86.384m
findings.quote: The deficit is escalating more significantly than originally anticipated, with an additional overspend resulting in a total in-year overspend in the region of £50m, which is most concerning. The Council will need access financial markets to borrow this financial year which will result in additional interest payable costs.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 202526 - Quarter One Revenue Budget Monitoring - Master Report (1)
findings.headline: 30% of £27.757m savings target undelivered or at risk, with only 70% achieved or on track
findings.detail: Of the £27.757m savings target, only 34% (£9.530m) is fully achieved and 37% (£10.255m) on track. £5.290m (19%) has deliverability issues and £2.685m (9.67%) is rated red. Red-rated items include £0.600m from CORE vacancy synergies (60% of which at risk), £0.520m procurement savings, £0.511m AI/automation savings, and £0.239m from delayed senior management restructure. findings.paper_title: Financial Year 202526 - Quarter One Revenue Budget Monitoring - Master Report (1)

Cost control measures remain in place but the S151 Officer explicitly states this position is not acceptable and signals unplanned mitigations are required. Current reserves could absorb this year but drawing from General Fund 'is not acceptable in the context of the quantum of savings already included in the MTFS for future years.'
findings.matters: An early-year overspend of this magnitude on a £568m budget indicates structural issues, not timing variances, and suggests the likelihood of reserve draw if not reversed—concerning for a lender evaluating financial resilience.
findings.figures: £6.748m overspend on £567.948m budget (1.2% variance)
findings.quote: The overall financial position  as forecast at Q1 is not tolerable, and it is incumbent on all managers and senior leaders to find mitigating solutions.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 Q1 Capital Budget Monitoring - Master Report (1)
findings.headline: Ongoing supply chain shortages and geopolitical volatility creating high risk to capital project costs and deliverability
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that shortages in supply chain (materials, components, labour) continue to create material risk. Construction material prices had stabilised but geopolitical environment is now making costs more volatile. The paper indicates this volatility is driving both cost increases (via necessity to lock in prices early) and delivery pace changes.
findings.matters: Supply chain volatility is a root cause of the cost overruns and reprofiling described above. Understanding the council's exposure to further cost inflation is material for debt service affordability.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this report
findings.quote: Shortages in supply chain in relation to materials, component parts, drivers and workforce continue to create high risk with deliverability and price for capital projects with impacts to the procurement process. Whilst the cost of construction material prices had stabilised, the geopolitical environment is making this more volatile and this will inevitably result in increased costs for the same provision.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 Q1 Capital Budget Monitoring - Master Report (1)
findings.headline: £73.024m of 2026/27 capital budget reprofiled to future years, with £34.158m of borrowing deferred
findings.detail: The council has moved £73.024m of capital expenditure from 2026/27 to future years to align with delivery forecasts. Of this, £36.703m was borrowing-funded. findings.matters: Reprofiling at this scale indicates the council is struggling to deliver its capital programme at forecast pace. The year-on-year increase in reprofiling (£31m more than 2025/26) suggests worsening delivery capacity.
findings.figures: £73.024m reprofiled to future years; £34.158m net borrowing deferred; £41.881m total variance
findings.quote: £73.024m of budget has been programmed into future years to align with projected timescales for delivery

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 Q1 Capital Budget Monitoring - Master Report (1)
findings.headline: Abbeyfield School expansion costs up £2.435m; Silverwood Phase 4 costs up approximately £2.5m following tender

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 Q1 Capital Budget Monitoring - Master Report (1)

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 Q1 Capital Budget Monitoring - Master Report (1)
findings.headline: MRP charge for 2026/27 forecast to exceed budget by £2.964m, with no explanation of the variance yet

findings.paper_title: Local SEND Reform Plan (1)
findings.headline: DfE approval of Local SEND Reform Plan not yet confirmed; failure to approve risks £86.384m deficit exposure
findings.detail: The paper states the council 'expects to hear in September or October whether the plan has been approved' but this remains unconfirmed as of the 16 September 2026 Cabinet meeting. The risks section explicitly warns: 'Failure to maintain credible local delivery would increase the council's exposure to DSG deficit risk... this could leave the council responsible for managing £86.384m of deficit... which would otherwise be mitigated through the national High Needs Stability Grant arrangements. This would place very significant pressure on the council's wider financial position and could require difficult decisions about resources across the organisation.'
findings.matters: A policy-dependent contingency on the order of £86m exists. The council cannot control whether DfE approves the plan or maintains that approval, making this a significant external dependency risk.
findings.figures: £86.384m deficit exposure if plan approval is not maintained
findings.quote: Failure to progress the plan would weaken the shared partnership approach... and could reduce confidence that Wiltshire is responding coherently to national and local SEND pressures. The most significant risk is financial: DfE approval of the submitted Local SEND Reform Plan is directly linked to government support for historic High Needs Block deficits, and failure to maintain credible local delivery would increase the council's exposure to DSG deficit risk... this could leave the council responsible for managing £86.384m of deficit... This would place very significant pressure on the council's wider financial position and could require difficult decisions about resources across the organisation.

findings.paper_title: Local SEND Reform Plan (1)
findings.headline: Creating 40 permanent posts with DfE grant funding that expires after 2029/30, creating unfunded liability risk
findings.detail: Approximately £3m of the 2026/27 investment (out of £3.354m total grant) is being spent on creating around 40 additional council posts. The grant is time-limited to the current reform period (through 2029/30). The plan explicitly states this creates a 'future workforce and financial sustainability consideration, particularly where roles are established before funding beyond the current reform period is confirmed.' The paper notes that 'further funding is anticipated in the following two financial years, although individual local authority allocations have not yet been confirmed.'
findings.matters: The council is recruiting permanent staff on temporary funding. Future funding is unconfirmed and the plan itself does not show how these roles will be sustained after grant funding ends. This creates contingent liabilities on the council's running costs.
findings.figures: ~40 additional posts; £3m of £3.354m grant (2026/27); estimated funding 2027/28 £5.864m and 2028/29 £6.646m but 'allocations have not yet been confirmed'
findings.quote: approximately £3m of the 2026/27 investment is expected to be spent primarily on staffing to deliver the Experts at Hand offer... These posts are expected to support delivery for the remaining 2.5 years of the current reform period and may need to continue beyond that point if the model becomes part of the council's ongoing SEND support infrastructure. This creates a future workforce and financial sustainability consideration, particularly where roles are established before funding beyond the current reform period is confirmed.

findings.paper_title: Local SEND Reform Plan (1)
findings.headline: Education, Health and Care Plan numbers have grown 72% in five years (4,158 to 7,149) with no stabilisation in sight
findings.detail: Wiltshire has experienced a 72% increase in EHCPs over five years, from 4,158 in March 2021 to 7,149 in March 2026. The financial model forecasts EHCP numbers will continue to rise. The council's original expectation to reach a balanced position in 2029 has slipped to 2031, and that only 'if support for children and young people was not to be compromised and if the national policy framework remained unchanged.' This represents a significant deferred solution rather than a resolved problem.
findings.matters: The core driver of the deficit is uncontrolled demand growth. Demand growth of 72% in five years drives cost forecasts that show deficits widening, not narrowing. The plan relies on demand-reduction measures (earlier intervention, inclusion) whose success is unproven.
findings.figures: 4,158 EHCPs in March 2021; 7,149 EHCPs in March 2026 (72% increase); balanced position shifted from 2029 to 2031
findings.quote: In Wiltshire, this pressure is reflected in a 72% increase in Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) over five years, from 4,158 in March 2021 to 7,149 in March 2026. The cumulative DSG deficit has grown significantly over the same period, driven by rising demand... In January 2025, Cabinet noted that the earliest realistic date for achieving an in-year balanced position had moved from 2029 to 2031.

findings.paper_title: Local SEND Reform Plan (1)
findings.headline: In-year High Needs Block deficits forecast to grow to £80.537m in 2027/28, with no solution beyond the statutory override period ending March 2028
findings.detail: The council forecasts in-year High Needs Block deficits of £68.984m in 2026/27 and £80.537m in 2027/28, meaning the cumulative deficit will reach £149.521m by end of March 2028. The paper states 'the government has indicated that there will be a level of support for deficits accrued up to the end of the statutory override period, but the details of those arrangements have not yet been confirmed.' The deficit is described as a 'significant financial risk to the council' requiring 'ongoing monitoring'.
findings.matters: The council's High Needs Block expenditure is forecast to exceed income by £149m over three years. The statutory override that lets councils run deficits expires in March 2028, and the government has not confirmed support arrangements beyond that point. This is an unresolved structural deficit.
findings.figures: £68.984m in-year deficit 2026/27; £80.537m in 2026/28; cumulative £149.521m by 31 March 2028; forecast expenditure £155.497m vs income £83.558m in 2026/27
findings.quote: The forecast indicates an expected in-year deficit of £68.984m in 2026/27 and £80.537m in 2027/28. This means that, by the end of the statutory override period on 31 March 2028, the council is forecast to have accrued a cumulative deficit of £149.521m. The government has indicated that there will be a level of support for deficits accrued up to the end of the statutory override period, but the details of those arrangements have not yet been confirmed.

findings.paper_title: Local SEND Reform Plan (1)
findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit of £86.384m is only mitigated if the DfE approves the plan, which has not yet happened
findings.detail: The council closed 2025/26 with a cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £86.384m. Access to the national High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of this historic deficit is conditional on DfE approval of the Local SEND Reform Plan. The paper states: 'there remains a significant financial risk if the plan is not approved by the DfE or if credible local delivery is not maintained.' If approval does not come through, the council faces the full £86.384m exposure.
findings.matters: This is an £86m contingent liability that swings the council's financial position by £86m depending on a single policy approval that remains uncertain and 'will need to be kept under review'.
findings.figures: £86.384m historic deficit; £40.200m Safety Valve payments; £18.445m council contribution; 90% grant coverage = £14.952m remaining council risk at 2027/28
findings.quote: All local authorities with a SEND deficit will be eligible in 2026/27 to receive a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of their high needs related DSG deficit accrued up to the end of the 2025/26 financial year... There remains a significant financial risk if the plan is not approved by the DfE or if credible local delivery is not maintained.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - LSRP Annex 5 - SEND Capital Revised Plan June 26 (1)
findings.headline: SEND demand pressures intensifying with EHCPs up 6.3% year-on-year and special school complexity increasing
findings.detail: EHCP numbers in Wiltshire reached 7,171 in June 2026 (+6.3% YoY). Special school populations increased 63% between 2019-2025. More significantly, the proportion of learners with Band 3 funding or higher (most complex needs) in maintained and academy special schools increased from 34% to 72% between 2021-2026. This growing complexity is driving demand for more capital investment in both mainstream and special school settings.
findings.matters: Rapidly growing and increasingly complex SEND demand may strain future capital budgets and borrowing requirements as the council must maintain sufficient places for a changing population.
findings.figures: 7,171 EHCPs (+6.3% YoY); special school population growth 63% (2019-2025); Band 3+ funding increased from 34% to 72% (2021-2026); 12-month rolling average for EHCP requests 97.5

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - LSRP Annex 5 - SEND Capital Revised Plan June 26 (1)
findings.headline: Total capital plan of £39.95M has £6.24M budget gap as future DfE funding not yet confirmed
findings.detail: SEND capital plan projects £39.95M spend across 2026-2029 against only £33.71M confirmed budget, creating a £6.24M gap. Council is relying on historical average allocation of £6.06M per annum to bridge the gap, but notes 'The amount and timing of DfE capital is often un-predictable'.
findings.matters: Significant capital plans rest on unconfirmed government funding with no certainty of receipt, creating risk of unplanned borrowing or project delays if allocations do not materialise.
findings.figures: Projected spend £39.95M; confirmed budget £33.71M; budget gap £6.24M; historical HNPCA average £6.06M per annum

findings.headline: Silverwood School phase 4 cost overruns leave insufficient budget for phase 5 refurbishment
findings.detail: Silverwood's £38.48M total budget allocated across three phases. findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 Q1 Capital Budget Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Supply chain and geopolitical volatility creating capital project cost and delivery risks
findings.detail: The council explicitly flags that shortages in supply chain (materials, components, drivers, workforce) continue to create high risk to capital project deliverability and price. It notes that while construction material costs had stabilised, 'the geopolitical environment is making this more volatile and this will inevitably result in increased costs for the same provision'. This is cited as the catalyst for bringing forward budget in some areas.
findings.matters: Acknowledged cost and delivery volatility means the capital programme remains exposed to external shocks. The paper does not quantify headroom for price escalation, suggesting the budget may be tight.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 Q1 Capital Budget Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Exeter House special school project (120 SEND places) delayed with unquantified cost implications
findings.detail: Exeter House, a conversion of a former boarding house in Ludgershall to deliver 120 special school places, is in detailed design stage and has 'incurred significant delays due to building issues'. The paper states this 'will have cost implications for the overall project' but does not quantify them. Delivery impact has been mitigated by temporary satellite provision (27 places at Wellington Lions Primary, Tidworth; 36 places at Pembroke Park Primary, Salisbury).
findings.matters: An unquantified cost variance on a major SEND project signals either incomplete project definition or building condition issues emerging. The paper does not say whether costs are contained in the budget or will overrun. Temporary places are more expensive than permanent provision.
findings.figures: 120 SEND places; scheme cost implications unquantified; temporary provision covers 63 places across two locations

The scheme has incurred significant delays due to building issues which will have cost implications for the overall project.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 Q1 Capital Budget Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Silverwood Phase 4 (special school) cost increase of approximately £2.5m and delays due to building issues and bat surveys
findings.detail: Refurbishment of older buildings at Silverwood's Rowde campus has seen total forecast expenditure increase by ~£2.5m due to building fabric issues and presence of bats in both Rowdeford House and Orchard Unit. Works that were to complete in August 2026 have slipped; Orchard Block now due December 2026. Temporary solution of five mobile classrooms (45 places) has been deployed. Rowdeford House works were withdrawn from current scheme due to complexity and cost of Grade II listed building.

findings.quote: The total forecast expenditure for Phase 4 has increased by circa £2.5m, which leaves less than £1m for Phase 5, the refurbishment and remodelling of Silverwood Trowbridge and Chippenham campuses.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 Q1 Capital Budget Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Abbeyfield School project cost increase of £2.435m due to planning, parking and inflation requirements
findings.detail: The Abbeyfield School expansion (150 places, originally planned for Sept 2025, now Sept 2027) has seen delivery costs increase by £2.435m following tender. Reasons cited are requirement to increase offsite highways contributions, construct all car parking in phase 1, purchase Biodiversity Net Gain credits, and inflation from geopolitical factors. The paper notes 'there is no impact to the current year budget or MTFS as these movements are within the budget line and are funded by CIL'.
findings.matters: Cost overruns on school expansions signal either weak project estimation or external pressures (planning, environmental, inflation) that could affect other schemes. The reliance on CIL to absorb the cost is important — it means no impact to borrowing this year but signals tighter CIL headroom.
findings.figures: £2.435m cost increase; scheme delayed from Sept 2025 to Sept 2027; funded by CIL
findings.quote: The delivery costs for this scheme have increased by £2.435m following the tender process. This is due to a requirement to increase contributions for offsite highways and construct all additional car parking in phase 1, to achieve planning consent, purchase of offsite Bid-Diversity Net Gain (BNG) credits and inflation due to geopolitics.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 Q1 Capital Budget Monitoring Report
findings.headline: £73.024m of capital budget reprofiled to future years, a variance of £41.881m from the original budget

The Q1 forecast stands at £218.506m against the £260.387m approved by Full Council. Officers note this is £31m more reprofiling than achieved in 2025/26, and the Q1 variance is 5x larger than last year's (£7.818m).
findings.matters: Large reprofiling signals either planning failures or delivery constraints. It defers borrowing costs and spreads debt service across more years. A lender needs to know whether this reflects genuine delivery challenges or optimism in budget setting.
findings.figures: £73.024m reprofiled; Q1 budget £218.506m vs original £260.387m; variance £41.881m
findings.quote: £73.024m of budget has been programmed into future years to align with projected timescales for delivery. This reprofiling has reduced the budget to £ 218.506m, a variance of £ 41.881m against the cabinet approved budget. This compares to the variance in 2025/26 of just £7.818m.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 Q1 Capital Budget Monitoring Report
findings.headline: MRP charge will overspend by £2.964m in 2026/27

findings.matters: MRP is a non-discretionary revenue cost driven by past borrowing decisions. An overspend here either diverts money from services or signals prior borrowing estimates were wrong.

findings.quote: the MRP charge for 2026/27 is forecast to be £24.382m against a budget of £21.418m, a variance of £2.964m. A review of the MRP calculation and methodology is to be carried out.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 - Q1 Revenue Budget Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Staffing cost pressures from pay award and inability to maintain vacancy factor across all services
findings.detail: Pay award of additional 0.3% (£0.793m in-year) has immediate impact and ongoing effect into future years' base budgets. Vacancy factor increased from 6.5% to 7.5% in 2026/27, but multiple services report inability to hold vacancies: Libraries cannot hold vacancies to keep buildings staffed, Corporate Directors' senior management restructure delayed preventing £0.239m saving delivery.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 - Q1 Revenue Budget Monitoring Report

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 - Q1 Revenue Budget Monitoring Report

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 - Q1 Revenue Budget Monitoring Report

findings.matters: Large-scale savings shortfall would require compensating cuts mid-year or general fund drawdown. The council has built a budget that relies on savings it cannot currently deliver.
findings.figures: £9.530m (34.33%) fully delivered; £10.255m (36.95%) on track; £5.290m (19.06%) at risk; £2.685m (9.67%) significant issues
findings.quote: For 2026/27 of the £27.757m savings targets £9.530m (34.33%) is assessed as having been fully delivered as at the end of June. £10.255m (36.95%) is forecast to be achieved by the end of the year. £5.290m (19.06%) is considered to have some deliverability risk, being that they may be achieved this year. This leaves £2.685m (9.67%) which are currently forecast to not be achieved by the end of the year showing significant risk.

findings.paper_title: Financial Year 2026-27 - Q1 Revenue Budget Monitoring Report
findings.headline: £6.748m unmitigated overspend at Q1 in a budget with £27m of required savings
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a net overspend of £6.748m for the year, which the S151 officer describes as 'not tolerable'. This is early in the year and expected to change, but no mitigation is currently in place. The overspend exists despite the budget already including £27.757m of required savings, creating structural vulnerability.
findings.matters: An unmitigated overspend of this scale so early in the year, combined with heavy reliance on savings delivery that is already at risk, indicates the council lacks sufficient headroom to absorb further pressures.
findings.figures: £6.748m overspend (1.2% of £567.948m budget); £27.757m savings target
findings.quote: The overall financial position as forecast at Q1 is not tolerable, and it is incumbent on all managers and senior leaders to find mitigating solutions.

findings.paper_title: Mid Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: Council flagging heightened economic uncertainty due to Middle East conflict and elevated inflation
findings.detail: The council notes that the conflict in the Middle East has significantly increased uncertainty in the UK economic outlook. CPI inflation has risen from 2.6% in February 2026 to 2.9% in July. The Bank of England remains divided on interest rate direction (three of nine MPC members voted to increase from 3.75% to 4.0%). The council states it will keep medium-term assumptions under review.
findings.matters: If inflation or interest rates exceed the council's assumptions, its financial position could deteriorate rapidly; this uncertainty flags higher scenario risk for lenders assessing the council's resilience.
findings.figures: CPI 2.6% (Feb 2026), 2.9% (July 2026); Bank Rate 3.75% since Dec 2025; 3 of 9 MPC members voted for 4.0% in July
findings.quote: The conflict in the Middle East has significantly increased the uncertainty surrounding the UK economic outlook.

findings.paper_title: Mid Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: Government finance settlement extends only to 2028/29, leaving 2029/30-2030/31 funding uncertain
findings.detail: The current Local Government Finance Settlement runs only through 2028/29, leaving funding for 2029/30 and 2030/31 unconfirmed. The council is assuming business rates will grow 2% annually in those years and Revenue Support Grant will remain flat, but these are unhedged assumptions with material risk.
findings.matters: Without certainty on government funding beyond 2028/29, the council cannot finalize its medium-term financial plan and multi-year savings programmes must be built on assumptions that may prove incorrect.
findings.figures: Settlement runs to 2028/29; assumptions for 2029/30-2031: RSG flat, business rates +2%
findings.quote: The current Local Government Finance Settlement (LGFS) only runs to 2028/29, meaning that funding for 2029/30 and 2030/31 is uncertain at this point.

findings.paper_title: Mid Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: Council shifting borrowing strategy to shorter-dated instruments citing elevated PWLB rates
findings.detail: PWLB rates (the council's primary long-term borrowing source) remain above the Bank of England's estimated neutral rate of 3.5%. In response, the council is reviewing its borrowing strategy and now favors shorter-dated PWLB borrowing (less than 5 years) and fixed-term local authority borrowing over longer-term instruments.
findings.matters: This signals the council considers long-term borrowing costs unattractive and is actively managing its debt structure in response to the interest rate environment, indicating elevated refinancing risk if rates move further.
findings.figures: Bank Rate 3.75% (static since December 2025); neutral rate estimate 3.5%; PWLB 5-year rate 5.20% (2026/27)
findings.quote: PWLB rates, the Council's primary source of long term borrowing, remain above the estimate of the longer-term neutral Bank Rate (3.5%). The Council is therefore reviewing the timing, maturity and structure of new borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Mid Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: National Living Wage rising 4.1% in 2026/27, significantly above general inflation
findings.detail: The National Living Wage is set at £12.71 per hour in 2026 and is projected to rise to £13.18 in 2027 (4.1% increase) and £13.60 in 2028 (3.7% increase), significantly outpacing the council's general inflation assumptions of 3.8% and 3.4%. The council is building in a 0.5% differential between NLW and inflation convergence over the MTFS period.
findings.matters: For labour-intensive services like adult social care and waste management, which represent material parts of county council budgets, NLW increases drive cost pressures independent of contract inflation that the council cannot control.
findings.quote: The National Living Wage (NLW) for 2026 is set at £12.71 per hour, and year on year increases continue to outpace increases in general inflation and local government pay awards.

findings.paper_title: Mid Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: Pay award assumptions revised upwards, creating £2.3m additional pressure in 2027/28
findings.detail: The 2026/27 pay award came in at 3.3%, 0.3% higher than the previous MTFS assumption of 3%, creating an in-year pressure of £0.7m. For 2027/28, the council is now assuming 3% pay inflation (previously assumed 2%) and 2.7% for 2028/29 (previously 2%), reflecting that pay awards in local government have consistently exceeded general inflation.
findings.matters: Pay costs are the largest budget line for councils; sustained elevation above inflation assumptions means the council faces ongoing cost pressures that will be difficult to absorb without further savings.
findings.figures: 2026/27 actual 3.3% vs budgeted 3%; 2027/28 revised to 3% (prior 2%); 2028/29 revised to 2.7% (prior 2%); in-year impacts £0.672m, £2.328m, £1.728m
findings.quote: The uplift for 2026-27 has now been agreed at 3.3%, so this creates an additional pressure on the base budget and MTFS (around £0.7m based on £0.23m per 0.1%).

findings.paper_title: Mid Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant declining 6.3% in 2027/28 and 5.8% in 2028/29, cutting £10.5m over three years
