findings.quote: MRP is being applied to some of this capital expenditure, as the business plan could not give the assurance necessary that the loan would be repaid in full.

findings.paper_title: Auditors Annual Report Wiltshire Local Government 2024-25 (final)
findings.headline: Future savings targets for 2026/27 will be the most significant the council has faced, but recent delivery has been uneven.
findings.detail: The council achieved £15.6m of £19.7m (79%) savings in 2024/25, with a £2.16m shortfall mainly in Adult Services. For 2025/26, the target is £15.4m with only 7.4% identified as high-risk. But auditors note that 2026/27 savings targets 'will be the most significant the Council has faced', and there is a cumulative budget gap of £5m over the medium-term financial plan period. Failure to deliver savings would force greater reliance on reserves or service cuts.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the sustainability of the savings plans the council is relying on to avoid larger deficits. Recent performance shows delivery shortfalls, particularly in Adult Services, and future targets are described as unprecedented.
findings.figures: 2024/25 savings achieved £15.6m of £19.7m target (79%); shortfall £2.16m; 2025/26 target £15.4m; 3-year cumulative budget gap £5m
findings.quote: Early indications are showing that savings targets for 2026/27 will be the most significant the Council has faced, and as a result, it needs to ensure that it can fully deliver identified savings targets or identify further mitigating actions in a timely way if the planned savings are not going to be achieved.

findings.paper_title: Auditors Annual Report Wiltshire Local Government 2024-25 (final)
findings.headline: The Council has revised its Safety Valve plan and now expects to reach in-year DSG balance in 2030/31, missing the original 2028/29 deadline by two years.
findings.detail: The Safety Valve Agreement was struck in March 2024 for 2023/24 to 2028/29, with the Department for Education providing £67m conditional on meeting financial targets. The Council has recognised targets were not being met and submitted a revised plan in December 2024 extending the in-year balance target to 2030/31. The DfE has not formally revised the agreement but has accepted the extension verbally. There is an ongoing risk the DfE could withdraw funding if the council continues to miss its targets.
findings.matters: The Safety Valve is the only external funding mechanism available to address the DSG deficit. If the DfE loses confidence in the council's delivery plan, funding could be withdrawn, leaving the council to cover the shortfall from its own resources.
findings.figures: Safety Valve funding £67m across 2023/24 to 2028/29; revised plan targets in-year balance by 2030/31 (two years later than original agreement)
findings.quote: The Council has recognised that financial targets identified within the Agreement are not being met, and a revised plan was submitted to the Department of Education (DofE) in December 2024 forecasting that in-year balance would be reached by 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Auditors Annual Report Wiltshire Local Government 2024-25 (final)
findings.headline: If the statutory override on DSG deficits is not extended beyond 2026/27, the Council's reserves will be insufficient to cover the projected deficit.
findings.detail: Currently, a national statutory override allows DSG deficits to be ring-fenced without requiring cash-backed reserves. The Council's general and earmarked reserves were £34.5m and £89.8m respectively at end 2024/25 (total £124.3m). But the DSG deficit is projected to reach £135.8m by 2027/28, and deficits will continue to accumulate. If the override lapses, the council would face an immediate balance sheet crisis.
findings.matters: This creates a hard deadline risk. The statutory override expires in 2026/27. If it is not extended, or if the DSG deficit grows faster than reserves can absorb, the council faces a solvency crisis that government may need to intervene to solve.
findings.figures: General fund reserves £34.5m, earmarked reserves £89.8m (total £124.3m) at end 2024/25; DSG deficit £61.2m end 2024/25, projected £135.8m by 2027/28; statutory override expires 2026/27
findings.quote: Currently, a national statutory override allows DSG deficits to be ring-fenced without requiring backing by cash reserves... If the override is not extended beyond 2026/27, when current legislation is due to expire, the Council's reserves would be insufficient to cover the projected DSG deficit.

findings.paper_title: Auditors Annual Report Wiltshire Local Government 2024-25 (final)
findings.headline: The Council must now borrow from financial markets in 2025/26 for the first time, driven by the cash impact of holding the DSG deficit.
findings.detail: The S151 Officer has indicated the Council will go out to the financial markets to borrow in 2025/26, incurring additional interest costs. This is a shift from the council's previous approach of minimising borrowing. The borrowing requirement is directly attributable to the DSG deficit's cash flow impact.
findings.matters: New borrowing increases the council's interest costs and debt servicing burden. For a lender, this signals deteriorating cash resilience and confirms that the DSG deficit is not just an accounting issue but a real cash problem.
findings.figures: Borrowing planned for 2025/26 (new activity)
findings.quote: The Council has taken an approach to minimise borrowing, however discussions with the S151 Officer have indicated that the Council will now have to go out to the financial markets to borrow in 2025/26, therefore resulting in additional interest payable costs.

findings.paper_title: Auditors Annual Report Wiltshire Local Government 2024-25 (final)
findings.headline: The Council will issue a disclaimed audit opinion and cannot achieve in-year assurance by the statutory backstop date because draft financial statements were not completed until October 2025.
findings.detail: Draft accounts were due 30 June 2025 but were not published until 7 October 2025. The Council has a pattern of missing statutory deadlines going back to 2020/21. Despite multiple assurances that statements were imminent, they were delayed by two months. The auditor will issue a disclaimed opinion (no opinion at all) rather than a qualified or unqualified opinion. This is an escalation from a prior key recommendation to a statutory recommendation.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the auditor cannot confirm the financial statements are accurate. For a lender, this means you cannot rely on published accounts for covenant monitoring or financial analysis. A pattern of missed deadlines suggests weak finance team capacity or governance.
findings.figures: Draft accounts deadline 30 June 2025; published 7 October 2025 (92 days late); pattern of delays 2020/21 through 2024/25; backstop date for audit completion 28 February 2026 (expected to be missed)
findings.quote: The Council published its draft 2024/25 financial statements on 7 October 2025 (delayed from 30 June 2025 deadline). Financial statements were still not produced until early September 2025, despite a number of assurances provided by the Council that they were imminent during the intervening period.

findings.paper_title: Auditors Annual Report Wiltshire Local Government 2024-25 (final)
findings.headline: Adult Services overspending has doubled year-on-year, from £6m to £13m, with no sign of control despite management action.
findings.detail: Adult Services overspend grew from £6.059m in 2023/24 to £12.97m in 2024/25—a 114% increase driven by demand and cost escalation. The council's net revenue overspend of £4.8m was largely funded from earmarked reserves. Q1 2025/26 forecasts continued large variances in Adult and Children's services, suggesting the budget-setting process is not capturing the real cost of demand.
findings.matters: A finance director faces a service that is spending twice its budget allocation. A lender needs to know whether the council has a realistic pathway to control this or whether it is simply hoping reserves can absorb it indefinitely.
findings.figures: Adult Services overspend 2023/24 £6.059m; 2024/25 £12.97m (doubled); net revenue overspend 2024/25 £4.8m; Q1 2025/26 forecast £6.5m overspend
findings.quote: In 2024/25, the variance in Adults services was the biggest pressure. The net overspend was £4.853m, however Adult services overspent by £12.97m. This is a continued trend from 2023/24, where the Council also overspent on Adults. The 2023/24 in-year variance for Adult services was £6.059m, and therefore this has doubled in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Auditors Annual Report Wiltshire Local Government 2024-25 (final)
findings.headline: DSG cumulative deficit has doubled to £61.2m and is forecast to reach £135.8m by 2027/28, exceeding Safety Valve Agreement targets.
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit increased dramatically from £28.7m at end 2023/24 to £61.2m at end 2024/25. The Council submitted a revised plan to the Department for Education in December 2024 forecasting in-year balance will not be reached until 2030/31, three years beyond the original agreement. Current projections for 2027/28 will exceed the Safety Valve Agreement's £70m target, creating a risk that the DfE could withdraw funding if the Council fails to meet targets.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council faces a structural, escalating deficit in its highest-demand services that is consuming reserves and forcing borrowing, with no agreed path to balance.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £61m end 2024/25 (up from £28.7m), projected £135.8m by 2027/28; original Safety Valve target £70m max by 2028/29; high needs reserves £18.2m
findings.quote: The cumulative DSG deficit stood at £61m at the end of 2024/25 after an in-year increase of £32.5m, and is projected to rise further to £135.78m by 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 - (final)
findings.headline: Expenditure completeness and year-end creditors testing abandoned; prior year control weaknesses still unresolved
findings.detail: Auditors identified presumed fraud risk in expenditure recognition based on prior control weaknesses identified by Deloitte in 2019-20 (lack of control over purchase orders and expenditure completeness). They planned to test controls and completeness but were unable to test in-year expenditure or year-end creditors due to the incomplete audit. Follow-up showed prior recommendations addressing this risk have not been fully implemented.
findings.matters: Inability to test expenditure and creditors leaves material spending areas unaudited, with known control weaknesses from 2019-20 still not fully addressed.
findings.figures: Prior risk identified: 2019-20 Deloitte audit
findings.quote: We remain unable to conclude on this risk. We have not been able to test in year expenditure and year end creditors.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 - (final)
findings.headline: Unable to complete testing of management override of controls; 36 journals left untested due to backstop deadline pressure
findings.detail: Auditors identified 36 high-risk journals for testing management override of controls (a mandatory fraud risk area in all audits). However, due to proximity to the backstop deadline, they agreed with management not to progress this testing. Instead, they will provide examples of appropriate evidence in a workshop to improve future audit efficiency.
findings.matters: Management override testing is foundational to audit quality and fraud detection. Leaving 36 journals untested means a critical audit area was not completed.
findings.figures: 36 journals identified for testing
findings.quote: Due to the number of journals identified for testing, being 36 in total, and the proximity to the backstop date, it was agreed with management that we would not progress this area of our audit testing. This means that we are unable to conclude on this risk on management override.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 - (final)
findings.headline: Oracle Fusion migration from November 2023 prevented auditors extracting detailed transactional listings for samples
findings.detail: Council migrated from SAP to Oracle Fusion in November 2023 (payroll in April 2024). In the first audit using the new system, auditors could not extract data at the correct detail level and spent considerable time trying to reconcile income, expenditure and grants to supporting listings. Issues were only resolved to 'subjective code level'; transactional listings needed for audit samples could not be obtained. IT resources had to be made available but the system limitations prevented completion.
findings.matters: The council cannot reliably extract and reconcile basic transaction data from its financial system, affecting the reliability of financial reporting and audit testing.
findings.figures: System migrated: November 2023. Payroll migrated: April 2024.
findings.quote: Data extraction at the correct level of detail has been difficult for the Council in the first year of audit with their new financial system, and this delayed the selection of our journal's samples. The Council were unable to provide detailed transactional listings that eliminated contra entries to support our detailed testing due to limitations in the financial ledger system.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 - (final)
findings.headline: Significant weaknesses identified in value for money arrangements; auditors not satisfied council has proper arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness
findings.detail: Under the NAO Code of Audit Practice, auditors assessed the council's arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in use of resources and identified significant weaknesses. The detailed commentary is in a separate Auditor's Annual Report. This is a formal VFM finding requiring reporting.
findings.matters: Significant weaknesses in VFM arrangements indicate systemic problems in how the council manages resources and delivers services.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: We identified a significant weaknesses in the Authority's arrangements and so are not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 - (final)
findings.headline: Statutory recommendation issued for lack of capacity and capability in finance function to meet statutory account deadlines
findings.detail: On 14 October 2025, auditors issued a statutory recommendation following significant delays in producing the 2024-25 draft financial statements. This repeats a prior key recommendation from 2023-24 on the same issue that has not been resolved, indicating persistent resource or capability constraints in the finance team.
findings.matters: Repeated inability to meet statutory deadlines signals systemic problems in the finance function's capacity or skills, affecting financial management across the council.
findings.figures: Statutory recommendation issued: 14 October 2025
findings.quote: We therefore issued the following statutory recommendation to the Audit and Governance Committee on 14 October 2025, 'The Council should urgently seek to address the capacity and capability constraints which have prevented it from publishing draft financial statements in a timely manner'.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 - (final)
findings.headline: Sixth consecutive disclaimed audit opinion after stopping 2024-25 audit before backstop deadline
findings.detail: Draft accounts were provided 5 September 2025 (significantly late) with full accounts on 7 October 2025. Auditors determined the progress made to date, work still required, and logistical challenges in obtaining transaction listings were too significant to meet the 27 February 2026 backstop deadline. They agreed with the s151 Officer and Director of Finance to stop the 2024-25 audit and refocus on 2025-26 planning. This is the council's sixth consecutive year of disclaimed opinions.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means auditors could not form any opinion on whether the financial statements are accurate. Lenders cannot rely on the published accounts.
findings.figures: Draft accounts provided: 5 September 2025. Full accounts: 7 October 2025. Audit commenced: 13 October 2025. Backstop deadline: 27 February 2026.
findings.quote: Consequently, we determined it was more appropriate to stop our 2024-25 audit and re-focus our efforts on planning for the 2025-26 audit, building upon our experience and the lessons learnt on the audit to date.

findings.paper_title: Report on Treasury Management Strategy 202526 Half Year ended 30 September 2025 (2)
findings.headline: Interest expenditure overrunning budget by £0.646m
findings.detail: The council is forecasting interest payments to exceed the approved budget by £0.646m in 2025/26, driven by the higher cost of servicing short-term borrowing taken this year. Investment income outperformance (£2.695m) partially offsets this, leaving a combined net underspend of £2.049m across the full interest budget.
findings.matters: Interest cost volatility indicates changed borrowing/investment conditions; ongoing overruns reduce financial headroom and reveal budget-setting gaps.
findings.figures: Interest expenditure overspend £0.646m; investment income outperformance £2.695m; combined net underspend £2.049m
findings.quote: The current forecast for interest expenditure for 2025/26 against budget is an overspend of £0.646m.

findings.paper_title: Report on Treasury Management Strategy 202526 Half Year ended 30 September 2025 (2)
findings.headline: £67.6m Stone Circle loans create credit and repayment risk
findings.detail: Wiltshire has lent £67.6m (forecast March 2026) to Stone Circle, a commercial entity, funded entirely by council borrowing. The report explicitly states that this arrangement 'creates additional credit risk for the Council' and that the council bears the full debt servicing burden regardless of whether Stone Circle repays.
findings.matters: The council's debt servicing depends on Stone Circle's performance and willingness to repay; no recovery mechanism if the company fails, and dividend income is uncertain.
findings.figures: Stone Circle loans outstanding £53.3m (March 2025); forecast £67.6m (March 2026); £14.3m drawn in 2025/26
findings.quote: Borrowing undertaken to fund capital expenditure, including the loans to Stone Circle, is owned and financed by the Council, regardless of whether any income is received from third party investments. This creates additional credit risk for the Council.

findings.paper_title: Report on Treasury Management Strategy 202526 Half Year ended 30 September 2025 (2)
findings.headline: £51.5m short-term borrowing taken as interest rate holding tactic
findings.detail: The council took new short-term external borrowing of £51.5m (maturing within 4–7 months) specifically because 'interest rates for longer-term borrowing remain higher than expected.' This is a deliberate delay in locking in long-term debt, betting on rate falls. The council states additional longer-term borrowing may occur 'dependent on forecasts for both cashflows and interest rates.'
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing carries refinancing risk; if rates don't fall as expected, the council faces higher permanent borrowing costs and pressure when loans mature.
findings.figures: New short-term borrowing £51.5m at 4.02–4.5%; maturing October 2025–March 2026
findings.quote: new short term external borrowing of £51.500 m was undertaken. As stated earlier in this report interest rates for longer-term borrowing remain higher than expected and the council therefore is taking an approach of taking short-term borrowing to bridge any cashflow deficits.

findings.paper_title: Report on Treasury Management Strategy 202526 Half Year ended 30 September 2025 (2)
findings.headline: Under-borrowed position cannot be sustained; High Needs DSG deficit pressuring cash position
findings.detail: Wiltshire holds £436.3m external borrowing against a capital financing requirement of £816.6m, meaning £380.2m is funded from cash reserves via internal borrowing. This historically prudent approach is being strained by the High Needs Dedicated Schools Grant deficit, which the council identifies as driving an 'ever increasing impact on the cash held by the council.' The council acknowledges this position 'will not be able to be maintained indefinitely.'
findings.matters: Sustainable under-borrowing depends on stable cash position; a shrinking DSG-driven cash buffer signals future external borrowing will be necessary, altering both debt trajectory and refinancing risk.
findings.figures: External borrowing £436.3m; CFR £816.6m; internal borrowing £380.2m
findings.quote: This position will not be able to be maintained indefinitely and the impact of the increasing deficit in the High Needs Dedicated Schools Grant is having an ever increasing impact on the cash held by the council.

findings.paper_title: Report on Treasury Management Strategy 2025-26 Half Year Ended 30 September 2025
findings.headline: Capital programme reduced by £38.652m from original budget
findings.detail: The revised capital programme is £214.743m against an original budget of £253.395m. Borrowing requirement fell from £117.656m to £88.339m. The reduction is driven by lower capital receipts (£78.273m budgeted, £1.314m now forecast) but higher than expected capital grants (£87.952m vs £0.481m budgeted).
findings.matters: Capital plan changes signal either improved planning or constrained ability to deliver. The sharp fall in capital receipts (sales of assets) is notable and may indicate property market weakness or asset disposal delays.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure reduced by £38.652m (15.3%); capital receipts fell from £78.273m to £1.314m; borrowing need reduced by £29.317m
findings.quote: The revised CFR is lower than the original estimate due to the reduction in the external borrowing required to support the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Report on Treasury Management Strategy 2025-26 Half Year Ended 30 September 2025
findings.headline: CCLA property fund holding has unrealised loss of £2.936m
findings.detail: The council's £20m investment in CCLA Local Authority Property Fund is valued at £17.064m, a decline of £2.936m. While IFRS9 statutory override defers revenue impact until 31 March 2029, the underlying asset has deteriorated. The council received only £0.190m dividend in Q1-Q2 (net return 3.81%), below initial expectations.
findings.matters: Asset value deterioration signals the council's investment strategy is suffering from market conditions. Even if revenue-protected now, eventual realisation of the loss or failure to recover the value is a cash event.
findings.figures: £20.000m purchased; £17.064m current valuation; £2.936m unrealised loss; £0.190m dividend received (3.81% net yield)
findings.quote: Due to a fall in property prices, the fund is currently valued at £17.064m. This difference does not represent a cost to the Council, as it is not charged to the Council's revenue account but held in a separate unusable reserve (until such time that the investment is sold (realised) or the statutory over-ride no longer applies).

findings.paper_title: Report on Treasury Management Strategy 2025-26 Half Year Ended 30 September 2025
findings.headline: Stone Circle loans (£67.576m forecast) create credit risk dependent on company performance
findings.detail: Wiltshire holds £67.576m in loans to Stone Circle (a council-owned company), funded entirely by council borrowing. The council explicitly acknowledges this creates additional credit risk because the loan repayment depends on the company's financial performance and dividend returns.
findings.matters: These are essentially leveraged investments. The council is borrowing on its credit to fund a third-party venture. If Stone Circle underperforms, the council still owns the debt.
findings.figures: £67.576m forecast total Stone Circle loans as at 31/03/2026 (from £53.313m at start of year)
findings.quote: Borrowing undertaken to fund capital expenditure, including the loans to Stone Circle, is owned and financed by the Council, regardless of whether any income is received from third party investments. This creates additional credit risk for the Council.

findings.paper_title: Report on Treasury Management Strategy 2025-26 Half Year Ended 30 September 2025
findings.headline: Under-borrowed position cannot be sustained indefinitely due to DSG deficits
findings.detail: The council currently uses cash reserves (£335m internal borrowing) rather than external borrowing. However, the council explicitly states this cannot be maintained indefinitely due to growing High Needs Dedicated Schools Grant deficits consuming cash. This signals future structural borrowing need.
findings.matters: The DSG shortfall is a legally mandated spending pressure. As it grows, the council's only response will be to borrow externally. A lender needs to understand that cash reserves providing current buffer will deplete.
findings.figures: £335.366m net internal borrowing position; DSG deficit described as having 'ever increasing impact'
findings.quote: This position will not be able to be maintained indefinitely and the impact of the increasing deficit in the High Needs Dedicated Schools Grant is having an ever increasing impact on the cash held by the council.

findings.paper_title: Report on Treasury Management Strategy 2025-26 Half Year Ended 30 September 2025
findings.headline: Council has taken £51.5m in new short-term borrowing to fund cashflow gaps
findings.detail: Rather than accessing long-term PWLB borrowing, Wiltshire has borrowed short-term from other councils and pension funds at 4.3-4.5%. The rationale given is that longer-term rates remain high and the council is deferring that decision. This creates refinancing risk when these loans mature.
findings.matters: Rolling short-term debt creates refinancing risk. When these loans mature (ranging from October 2025 to March 2026), the council will need to either repay or renew, potentially at different rates. This is a tactical bet on interest rates.
findings.figures: £51.500m in short-term loans taken during the half-year
findings.quote: Due to the overall financial position and the underlying need to borrow for capital purposes (the CFR), new short term external borrowing of £51.500m was undertaken. As stated earlier in this report interest rates for longer-term borrowing remain higher than expected and the council therefore is taking an approach of taking short-term borrowing to bridge any cashflow deficits.

findings.paper_title: Report on Treasury Management Strategy 2025-26 Half Year Ended 30 September 2025
findings.headline: Interest expenditure is overrunning budget by £0.646m
findings.detail: The council forecast a cost overspend on interest payments for 2025-26. This is a material pressure, particularly notable because interest rates were falling during this period (Bank of England cut from 4.50% to 4.00%), yet costs are still higher than anticipated. If rates had not fallen this sharply, the overspend could be larger.
findings.matters: Interest cost increases directly impact the council's revenue account and debt servicing capacity. Overruns suggest either conservative budgeting has failed or the council faces unanticipated cost pressure.
findings.figures: £0.646m overspend forecast against budget for 2025/26
findings.quote: The current forecast for interest expenditure for 2025/26 against budget is an overspend of £0.646m.

news_drafts.headline: Wiltshire expects £90.5m special needs grant on 30 November, with about £10m still to find by March 2028
news_drafts.lead:
Wiltshire Council expects a £90.5m government grant on 30 November 2026 related to its deficit on special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) spending, its mid-year treasury report to Cabinet says. The grant is subject to audit. The paper says it will repay short-term loans from other councils maturing in November and December, and elsewhere gives £75m of temporary loans as the main use. The budget monitoring report puts the grant at £90.326m and says the £3.942m left over "will be set aside to offset deficits accrued before the end of the statutory override period (31st March 2028)". The override is a government rule that keeps a schools-funding deficit off a council's main balance sheet.

The deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, stood at £86.384m at the end of 2025/26, after government Safety Valve payments and the council's agreed contribution. The surplus arises because that contribution was higher than the 10% the new grant conditions require. For 2026/27 the council forecasts a £5.785m overspend in high needs, the part of school funding for SEND, up £1.410m from quarter one. A £5.698m early years underspend reduces the overall deficit, which is forecast at £1.458m above the plan submitted to the Department for Education. Placement and support costs will be validated before quarter three.

The treasury paper says the deficit is having an "ever-increasing impact on the cash held by the council". It puts the council's under-borrowed position at £219.245m at 30 September 2026 and says that cannot be maintained indefinitely. The council's chief finance officer estimates it "will need to find approximately £10m" by 31 March 2028, assuming government support for 90% of the deficit. Arrangements for deficits accrued in 2026/27 and 2027/28 are not yet confirmed.

news_drafts.headline: Wiltshire expects £90.3m high needs grant at end of November after government approves SEND plan
news_drafts.lead:
The government approved Wiltshire Council's Local SEND Reform Plan in October 2026, releasing a High Needs Stability Grant that the council estimates at £90.326m and expects to be paid at the end of November. The council's dedicated schools grant (DSG) deficit, an overspend on the government grant that funds schools, was £86.384m at the end of 2025/26. The quarter two budget monitoring report estimates a surplus of £3.942m after the grant. That sum is to be set aside against deficits before the statutory override, a temporary government rule keeping such deficits off the main balance sheet, ends on 31 March 2028.

The same report forecasts a £5.785m overspend in high needs, the part of the grant for children with special educational needs and disabilities. That is £1.410m worse than at quarter one. An underspend in early years of £5.698m, and one in the central blocks, offset it. The in-year DSG position is a £0.087m underspend after a planned transfer from the deficit reserve. The deficit is forecast to be £1.458m above the plan submitted to government.

The council estimates it will need to find approximately £10m to cover the cumulative deficit by 31 March 2028, assuming government support for 90% of it under the agreed plan. The chief finance officer's commentary states that without an extension to the override, reserves would not cover the predicted cumulative deficit. The mid-year treasury management report says the growing high needs deficit is having "an ever-increasing impact on the cash held by the council", and cites it as one cause of the interest overspend.

news_drafts.headline: Wiltshire says its high needs reserve will not cover the schools-funding deficit projected for March 2028
news_drafts.lead:
Wiltshire Council's high needs reserve will not be enough to meet the schools-funding deficit projected for March 2028, according to the strategic risk summary put to its Audit and Governance Committee on 6 October. The council says overspending on support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) is exceeding the high needs allocation, the part of its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) set aside for that support.

The council has submitted a SEND Reform Plan to the Department for Education. Under it, 90% of the deficit as at 31 March 2026 would be written off, and the remaining 10% met from the council's high needs reserve, money it has put aside for that purpose. The paper states: "The council's earmarked reserve is not sufficient to meet the projected deficit at the end of the statutory override." The statutory override is a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, and it ends in March 2028. The papers say no government guidance has yet explained how deficits built up between March 2026 and March 2028 will be handled.

The council has also changed how it describes the risk. Its strategic risk on demand for education, health and care plans, the legal documents setting out a child's support needs, has been renamed, redefined and rescored. In the council's words, it "now focuses more broadly on provision of support for children with SEND within available budgets."
